newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Building bears return on fresh German gloom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Building bears return on fresh German gloom.

text.p: British building material shares have had a rocky ride, beginning the week as star stocks on hopes the worst was over for the industry but ending up on the run from the bears once again.
RMC Group Plc and Redland Plc both surged early in the week, touching new year highs on hopes that disastrous conditions in the key German market had bottomed out.
But everything changed on Thursday when RMC reported a 26.5 percent collapse in half year profits to 95.8 million pounds ($148.8 million) and warned a German recovery was not imminent.
The news sent RMC's shares crashing 42 1/2 pence to 1,110, wiping out the gains of the week.
Redland, which reports next Thursday, was also softer on the news. Both groups get around 40 percent of sales and profits from Germany.

RMC recovered some of its poise on Friday and closed 14-1/2 up at 1,125, but it was still well off its high of 1,199 at the start of the week. Redland was at 455-1/2 pence, compared with its new 478 high hit on Monday.
Many sector analysts had been expecting a more upbeat outlook from RMC on Germany. But its chief executive, Peter Young, made it clear that the downturn would continue into 1997.

"In Germany we would not expect the volumes in the second half to be as badly down as in the first half. But I don't want to be too optimistic. There may be a slight decline in volumes of one or two percentage points (in 1997)," he said.
The building material groups have been rocked by a combination of poor winter weather across Europe delaying many building projects and weak markets.
Simon Brown, an analyst at UBS, said: "Germany remains a tough market for this year and next."
The late August cut in German interest rates by the Bundesbank was bigger than expected and raised hopes of an earlier rebound, said analysts.
But after basking in the boom years of building which followed Germany's reunification, the construction industry is still suffering from a recessionary hangover.

West Germany is seen holding out some hope for a slow steady recovery, but some analysts were pessimistic about east Germany. One key factor cited is that east German housing could see further pressure in 1997 because of the removal of a layer of tax breaks for building in this sector.
This benefit, relating to depreciation allowances, reduces the incentive to build housing there said one analyst.

Spending on infrastructure is also tight as governments in Germany and the other major continental European market, France, clamp down on expenditure in a bid to meet the economic criteria for joining European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Arend Dikkers, analyst and director at Salomon Brothers, said the cut in infrastructure spending was "very clearly EMU-related" and a natural target for governments.
"It's painfully obvious that saving on infrastructure is easiest -- roads and rail projects don't have votes, as opposed to people on welfare." ($1=.6439 Pound)
